lesson.title: The Wrong Answer, Said Confidently: Inside the Asch Conformity Study
lesson.summary: In a series of experiments in the early 1950s, Solomon Asch showed that a surprising number of people would publicly agree with an obviously incorrect group judgment on a simple visual task, becoming the single most famous laboratory demonstration of conformity.
lesson.body:
The concept of conformity, covered in the previous section, gets much more concrete once you walk through the specific experiment most responsible for putting it on the map. Solomon Asch designed his studies in the early 1950s specifically to test conformity under conditions where there should have been very little reason for anyone to conform at all, since the task involved was simple and unambiguous rather than the kind of genuinely uncertain judgment used in Sherif's earlier autokinetic effect study.

The design itself is a good example of the controlled, carefully operationalized methods that characterize the scientific study of psychology more broadly. A single real participant was seated in a small group along with several other people who were actually confederates working with the experimenter, though the participant believed everyone in the room was an ordinary participant like themselves. The group was shown a "standard" line and three comparison lines and asked, one at a time and out loud, to say which comparison line matched the standard line in length. The task was designed to be extremely easy: when people made this judgment alone, they answered correctly nearly all the time. On most trials the confederates answered correctly too, but on certain designated "critical" trials, the confederates had been instructed in advance to unanimously give the same, obviously incorrect answer, and the real participant always answered near the end of the group, after hearing the confederates' unanimous wrong response.

The results are usually summarized in two ways. Looking at individual trials, roughly one third of the real participants' responses on critical trials matched the incorrect majority rather than the participant's own eyes. Looking at people rather than trials, a substantially larger share, commonly cited as around three quarters of participants, conformed to the incorrect majority at least once across the several critical trials they experienced, even though there was also a great deal of individual variation, since a meaningful number of participants never conformed at all. In interviews afterward, many participants privately reported knowing the majority's answer had been wrong, which is a strong sign that Asch's results mostly reflect normative social influence, the discomfort of publicly standing out from the group, discussed in the previous section, rather than informational social influence, since the task was not actually ambiguous.

Asch also tested variations that echo the factors discussed in the general conformity section: conformity dropped sharply when even one confederate broke from the unanimous majority and gave the correct answer, showing that a single ally can be enough to make dissent feel possible again, and conformity generally increased with the size of the unanimous majority only up to a modest limit before leveling off. It is also important to place Asch's specific numbers in proper context rather than treating them as a fixed law of human nature. Later research, including cross cultural comparisons and meta-analyses conducted decades after the original studies, most notably work by Rod Bond and Peter Smith in the 1990s, has found that conformity rates on Asch type tasks vary meaningfully across cultures, tending to run higher in more collectivist cultures that place greater value on group harmony, and some analyses suggest conformity rates in individualist Western countries have also shifted somewhat across the decades since Asch's original studies. The core finding, that ordinary people will sometimes override the clear evidence of their own senses under group pressure, has held up well, but the exact rate at which that happens is better understood as sensitive to cultural and historical context than as a single universal number.
